clue.text: Structures of organizations elevated in groups

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the word for groups

parts.note: sets are groups or collections
up means raised or elevated

explanation.surface: An observation about how corporate hierarchies are raised up within collective bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: A setup is the way an organization is arranged, its structure.

clue.text: Lake Curzon ?

definitions.meaning: the largest of North America's Great Lakes
Lord Curzon was mocked in verse as a most ... person

explanation.surface: A lake named after a Viceroy of India.
explanation.walkthrough: An Oxford rhyme said of George Nathaniel Curzon: 'My name is George Nathaniel Curzon, I am a most superior person.'
explanation.definitionFit: One of the Great Lakes, and the haughty quality the famous rhyme gave Lord Curzon.

clue.text: "—— has done his worst" (Macbeth)

parts.note: a quotation with its first word blanked: Macbeth says of the murdered Duncan that betrayal of the king has done his worst

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Macbeth with its subject missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash before 'has'; the missing word completes Macbeth's 'Duncan is in his grave ... has done his worst'.
explanation.definitionFit: Betrayal of one's sovereign is the crime Macbeth names as having done its worst to Duncan.

clue.text: He gets the best seat

parts.note: the person who takes the chair at a meeting occupies the place of honour

explanation.surface: A remark about who sits in the finest chair.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a body or meeting sits in the chair, the seat of authority.

clue.text: Avuncular overtures?

parts.note: an uncle is slang for a pawnbroker, whose friendly offers are loans of money; overtures are also approaches made to someone

explanation.surface: A kindly uncle making friendly approaches.
explanation.walkthrough: The pawnbroker is called 'uncle', and what he makes are loans; the word for loans is also the word for amorous or friendly approaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtures made to a person and sums lent ahead of time share one word: approaches and loans.

clue.text: Economic measure by clockwork

parts.note: a scheme to save fuel and light carried out by putting the clocks forward an hour

explanation.surface: A thrift policy run by machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Summer time, when clocks go forward so evenings stay light, was brought in to save fuel.

clue.text: About to give change for a tanner, almost

indicators.note: giving change for something turns it into another form, here a rearranged one
almost says the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone is about to hand over coins in exchange for a sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner is old British slang for a sixpence coin. 'almost' cuts TANNER to TANNE, and 'to give change for' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word meaning concerning or regarding, chiefly Scots and legal.

clue.text: The elegancy, facility, and golden of poesy " (L. L. Lost)

definitions.text: The elegancy, facility, and golden of poesy " (L. L. Lost)

parts.words: The elegancy, facility, and golden of poesy " (L. L. Lost)

explanation.surface: A line from Love's Labour's Lost with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash after 'golden'; the missing word is the rhythmic fall of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhythmic rise and fall of verse, which Holofernes calls golden.

clue.text: Gigantic in the playground

parts.note: the giant ... was playground apparatus, a pole with ropes children swung round on

explanation.surface: Something huge spotted where children play.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'giant stride' was a common piece of playground equipment: a tall pole with ropes hanging from a rotating top.
explanation.definitionFit: A long step; with giant in front it named a piece of playground equipment.

clue.text: Such poseurs, those Anglo Saxon messengers ?

definitions.meaning: in Through the Looking-Glass the messenger Haigha strikes Anglo-Saxon attitudes

explanation.surface: Showing-off types compared to Old English couriers.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's messengers Haigha and Hatta are described as 'Anglo-Saxon messengers' with 'Anglo-Saxon attitudes', so they strike poses.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who adopt affected poses, as Carroll's messengers adopt odd attitudes.

clue.text: Soon feel affronted by having to work around

indicators.note: around says the word for work goes round the outside of the other piece

parts.note: to ply is to work at a trade
to resent something is to feel affronted by it

explanation.surface: Someone will shortly be offended at being made to work around something.
explanation.definitionFit: Presently is an older synonym for shortly, in a little while.

clue.text: It flourishes no doubt in Kirkwall

definitions.text: It flourishes no doubt in Kirkwall

parts.words: It flourishes no doubt in Kirkwall
parts.note: a shrub with white flowers grows anywhere, and an office-bearer of the Scottish Presbyterian church flourishes in a town whose name begins with kirk, Scots for church

explanation.surface: A remark on what grows well in Kirkwall, the chief town of Orkney.
explanation.walkthrough: Kirkwall is the main town of Orkney; its first syllable, kirk, is Scots for church, where lay officials of the Church of Scotland serve.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a flowering shrub and a lay official of a Presbyterian kirk.

clue.text: William Tell was a noteworthy hero of his

definitions.text: William Tell was a noteworthy hero of his

parts.words: William Tell was a noteworthy hero of his
parts.note: noteworthy means set to musical notes: the Swiss archer is the hero of an Italian composer's last opera

explanation.surface: A claim about a writer's most famous character, the Swiss archer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer wrote the opera Guillaume Tell in 1829.

clue.text: Had a sing-song ?

parts.note: a sing-song is a jolly singing party, but also a monotonous rising and falling voice, the way a priest chants

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed a session of group singing.
explanation.definitionFit: To recite in a chanting, level voice is to speak in a sing-song way.

clue.text: For a big cat, he's very light!

definitions.meaning: the snow leopard of Central Asia has an old name of its own
a small unit of weight, one sixteenth of a pound

explanation.surface: A large feline, oddly described as weighing next to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow leopard is also known by this name, which is also a tiny imperial weight of about 28 grams.

clue.text: Like the self-made man, with his plate still empty?

definitions.text: Like the self-made man, with his plate still empty?

parts.words: Like the self-made man, with his plate still empty?
parts.note: a self-made man got no assistance, and a diner with an empty plate has had no helping of food

explanation.surface: A self-made man pictured sitting at table before being served.
explanation.definitionFit: Without assistance, and also not yet served a portion, two senses of not given help.

clue.text: Thinly plated

parts.note: made up of thin layers or plates, a botanical and zoological term

explanation.surface: Something covered with a thin coat of metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Formed of thin layers or scales, from Latin lamella, a small plate.

clue.text: Demonstrates in favour of exams ?

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
tests are examinations

explanation.surface: Someone marches in support of school examinations.
explanation.definitionFit: To protest is to demonstrate against something publicly.

clue.text: They depart in royal company

parts.note: recalls Kipling's Recessional: the tumult and the shouting dies, the military leaders and the Kings depart

explanation.surface: Courtiers leaving alongside the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Kipling's hymn Recessional, where these leaders go out with the Kings, so their company is royal.
explanation.definitionFit: Military commanders go out alongside the Kings in the Kipling line, which is the royal company meant.

clue.text: Has a high opinion of both sire and dam

indicators.note: both pools the letters of the two words named, which are then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone thinks well of each parent of a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sire' and 'dam' are a horse's father and mother; 'both' throws all their letters together to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To esteem or look up to someone.

clue.text: Harpagon, for example

parts.note: Harpagon is the title character of Moliere's comedy L'Avare, a hoarder of money

explanation.surface: Naming a figure from French comedy as a type.
explanation.definitionFit: Harpagon is the stingy hoarder of Moliere's play The Miser, the classic skinflint.

clue.text: Home of Lady Webster of the lovely face

definitions.text: Home of Lady Webster of the lovely face

parts.words: Home of Lady Webster of the lovely face
parts.note: Tennyson's Lady weaves a magic web, and Lancelot says she has a lovely face

explanation.surface: Asking where a titled Mrs Webster with a pretty face lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Webster' is not a surname: it is an old word for a weaver, and Tennyson's Lady weaves her web. Lancelot ends the poem: 'She has a lovely face.'
explanation.definitionFit: The island castle in Tennyson's poem where the weaving Lady lives.

clue.text: Jack's accustomed to being reviled

explanation.surface: A sailor is used to being insulted.
explanation.definitionFit: To be abused is to be insulted and treated with scorn.

clue.text: "Young Italy "?

explanation.surface: A reference to Giuseppe Mazzini's nineteenth-century political movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for little children, babies, is literally the young of Italy.

clue.text: Trips awkwardly after a bow ?
